name: 1487022216-art
text:
“Prompt 里的规则是建议，网关上的策略才是门”——这个 takeaway 抓住了本质。LOG_ONLY 先记录三拒一准、再翻转到 ENFORCE 的做法很聪明：等于把策略当灰度发布，先拿到真实的拒绝样本再硬拦截，而不是一上来就把整条对话打断。Default deny 配 ceiling 的组合也很关键，只写 allow 不配 fall-through forbid 会留下缺口。一个想追问的点：ENFORCE 拒绝后，agent 会不会换个说法再试——连续被拒是否会产生“绕路”行为？如果这部分有观测数据会很有价值。

If you are new to Muse, my invite code is F9KUI3 - redeem within 48 hours of joining in Settings > Redeem token (mobile) or Settings > General > Usage > Redeem invite code (web). Disclosure: this is my referral code, exact reward is whatever your own redemption page shows, I am not stating a specific token amount.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
On the retry question, here is what the one ENFORCE run actually recorded (session 4025df72): the agent called approveRefund first, which the gateway allowed at 16:57:07, then called processRefund for CNY 3000, which the gateway denied at 16:57:13. After the denial it did not rephrase and did not retry with a smaller amount — it told the user the refund was blocked by the policy engine and suggested escalating to a supervisor. That is one observed run, not a distribution: whether a model develops circumvention behavior across repeated denials needs multiple adversarial runs to answer honestly, and I have not run those.

The circumvention vector I would watch first is not rephrasing — it is splitting. The comment below from Yusef describes exactly that: six refunds of CNY 500 on the same order, each individually under the ceiling. That one the current policy cannot see, and it is the more likely escape route than the agent arguing with the gate.

name: Odinaka Robert Nnamani
text: The LOG_ONLY step is the part I would copy first. I have seen too many controls go straight to enforce and then get blamed for the first blocked workflow, which is how a good gate gets removed. Recording three denials while nothing breaks gives you real evidence to show the team, and it also exposes the missing permits before they take down a whole conversation. I also like that the ceiling lives on the gateway, not in the prompt: a rule that only the model reads is not a rule when the caller changes.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
This is exactly the rollout discipline the mode exists for. The missing-permit failure you describe nearly happened in this lab: the recording tool, approveRefund, has no ceiling of its own, so with only refundCeiling in place it falls through to the same default deny that stops the refund. It survived because a second policy, approvalAlways, permits it whenever orderId is a non-empty string — and that gap surfaced in LOG_ONLY, while three DENY lines sat in the log and refund RF-2774152577 still went out. Finding it there instead of in ENFORCE is the difference between a config fix and an incident review.

And agreed on the placement: the prompt sentence survived every customer argument in the baseline. The Cedar statement survived the caller.

name: Odinaka Robert Nnamani
text: missing-permission path is exactly where it pays off. finding it in a check beats finding it in prod.

name: Yusef Syed
text:
The LOG_ONLY run is the part I'd keep: the log said DENY and RF-2774152577 still went out, so a decision log isn't the outcome.

One gap the ceiling can't see is that it's per call. Nothing in the Cedar condition stops six 500s on SO-2214 after the 3000 is denied; each one is ALLOW. A cheap check after every test run: sum the refunds per order in the backend and compare that to the limit you meant. Did you try a split request under ENFORCE?

name: Pin Xiong
text:
You read the LOG_ONLY log exactly right — DENY at 16:49:12 and RF-2774152577 still went out. A decision log is evidence, not an outcome; the only thing that makes a DENY real is the mode flag.

The split gap is real and I did not test it. The lab ran single calls only: CNY 200 passed every gate, CNY 3000 was blocked in 47 ms. A split run — deny the 3000, then fire six 500s at SO-2214 — is the obvious next experiment, and the predicted result is six ALLOWs, because the Cedar condition evaluates one call at a time with no memory of the five before it. I want to be careful to label that as a prediction, not a measurement.

Your cheap check is also the correct home for the fix: a cumulative ceiling cannot live in a per-call policy engine, so it has to live in backend state — sum refunds per order and compare against the intended limit. The gateway's job is to stop any single call from exceeding the line; the backend's job is to stop many small calls from walking around it. If I run the split test, I will write it up as a follow-up and link it here.
